items.label: f04-health-is-not-snapshot
items.front: What the refund health counts do NOT promise
items.back: They are separate CountAsync queries, not one atomic snapshot, so a worker can change rows between them. A retryable count means eligible by the attempt rule, not that the provider will accept the refund or that the worker is healthy.
The refund query has no `OrderBy` (`Worker.cs:26`); add one so recovery order is deterministic and old refunds are not starved behind a hot set.

items.label: f01-duplicated-twelve
items.front: Where does the 12-attempt limit live, and why is that a risk?
items.back: It is a literal in Worker.cs:24 (payment sagas), Worker.cs:26 (refund selection) and ReadApi.cs:70, 72-73 (health counts). Changing the worker limit without ReadApi would silently mislabel refunds; extract one shared constant.

items.front: 2: Refunds reach "needing retry" in seconds, not hours.
items.back: `ProcessRefund` increments `Attempts` on failure (`Worker.cs:150`) and the selection has no backoff filter (`Worker.cs:26`); with a 1.5 s tick (`Worker.cs:34`) a failing refund is stuck after about 18 seconds. Payment sagas, by contrast, delay by `min(120, attempts*5)` s (`Worker.cs:125`). The health card is accurate, but the policy behind it deserves a backoff.

items.label: f02-refund-capacity
items.back: refunded + refundPending <= captured. A refund request reserves capacity in refundPending; only a confirmed provider refund moves it into refunded. Provider events wake reconciliation instead of inventing financial state.

items.label: f03-asymmetric-fixtures
items.front: Why do the two merchants in RefundHealthTests get different expected counts?
items.back: So a missing MerchantId predicate cannot pass by accident. Merchant A expects 4/2/2 and merchant B 2/1/1; dropping the scope from one query changes A's numbers and an assertion fails.

items.prompt: Someone changes retryableRefunds to Attempts <= 12 and leaves stuckRefunds as it is. What happens to a pending refund at 12?

choices.text: Nothing visible changes, because the worker still stops at twelve
It lands in both groups, so the parts add up to more than the total
Only the retryable count changes; the stuck group loses that row
It drops out of both groups, so the parts add up to less than the total

choices: Nothing visible changes, because the worker still stops at twelve
It lands in both groups, so the parts add up to more than the total
Only the retryable count changes; the stuck group loses that row
It drops out of both groups, so the parts add up to less than the total

items.explanation: Attempts <= 12 and Attempts >= 12 are both true at 12, so the partitions overlap. A single pending refund at exactly 12 exposes it; the correct split is < 12 versus >= 12.

items.explanation: healthStats adds help: "Open the order and use the authorized Retry refund action." and Panels renders it as the card title. The card is guidance; it performs no mutation and adds no endpoint.

items.prompt: One pending refund has exactly 12 attempts. Which health counts does it add to?

choices.text: None of them, because the worker no longer selects that row
Only stuckRefunds; the pending total leaves out exhausted rows
pendingRefunds and stuckRefunds, but not retryableRefunds

Only stuckRefunds; the pending total leaves out exhausted rows
pendingRefunds and stuckRefunds, but not retryableRefunds
pendingRefunds and retryableRefunds, as 12 is still eligible

items.explanation: pendingRefunds needs only State == "pending"; retryableRefunds needs Attempts < 12; stuckRefunds needs Attempts >= 12. A row at 12 fails the first partition and passes the second, and it is still pending.

items.prompt: A request carries owner A's account id with merchant B's merchant claim. What does the health endpoint do?

It returns merchant A's counts and ignores the merchant claim

items.explanation: Session.Account looks up an account with BOTH the id and the merchant from the claims (x.Id == id && x.MerchantId == merchant). No such account exists, so it throws DomainError("unauthorized", ..., 401) before the health branch runs.

2, as the other merchant's rows at 12 are all succeeded
4, as both of merchant B's rows at 12 are added to A's

items.explanation: Without the scope, the query counts every pending row with Attempts >= 12 in the table: A's 12 and 13 plus B's pending 12. B's succeeded 12 still fails the state predicate and B's 11 fails the attempt predicate. The asymmetric fixture makes this visible.

items.prompt: command() in src/lib/client.ts gets a 503 back. What happens to the Idempotency-Key it sent?

choices.text: It is kept, and a retry of the same payload reuses that key
It is cleared, and command() retries the request on its own
It is kept in memory only, never written to sessionStorage
It is cleared, and the next try sends a brand-new random key

choices: It is kept, and a retry of the same payload reuses that key
It is cleared, and command() retries the request on its own
It is kept in memory only, never written to sessionStorage
It is cleared, and the next try sends a brand-new random key

items.explanation: The key is stored in pendingKeys and sessionStorage under a digest of operation + canonical payload. The catch clears it only for an ApiError with status < 500 that is not 429, because a 5xx may already have committed. command() never retries by itself.

items.explanation: The succeeded row is excluded everywhere. Of the four pending rows, 0 and 11 are below 12 (retryable) and 12 and 13 are at or above it (stuck). The test asserts exactly 4, 2 and 2.

items.prompt: How does the architecture define sellable available stock?

choices.text: onHand + transit - held
onHand + inbound - reserved
onHand - reserved - held
onHand - held - transit

choices: onHand + transit - held
onHand + inbound - reserved
onHand - reserved - held
onHand - held - transit

items.explanation: available = onHand - reserved - held, and database constraints forbid negative terms. Checkout raises reserved, capture moves reserved into held, and neither transit nor expected supplier goods are sellable.

items.prompt: A refund's provider call fails every time. About how soon does it reach "Refunds needing retry", and why?

choices.text: About 6 min: each refund retry backs off by 5 s per attempt
About 12 min: the worker retries refunds once every minute
About 18 s: it is retried each 1.5 s tick with no backoff
Never: the worker gives up at 11 attempts and leaves it there

choices: About 6 min: each refund retry backs off by 5 s per attempt
About 12 min: the worker retries refunds once every minute
About 18 s: it is retried each 1.5 s tick with no backoff
Never: the worker gives up at 11 attempts and leaves it there

items.explanation: The refund selection is State == "pending" && Attempts < 12 with no time filter, the loop delays 1500 ms, and each failure does Attempts++. Twelve failures take about 18 s. The min(120, attempts*5) backoff applies to payment sagas, not refunds.

items.prompt: A refund has State "succeeded" and 20 attempts. How does it affect the three refund counts?

choices.text: It adds to none of them, since every refund count requires pending
It adds to retryableRefunds, because success resets the counter
It adds to stuckRefunds alone, as its attempts are above twelve
It adds to pendingRefunds and stuckRefunds, like a pending row

choices: It adds to none of them, since every refund count requires pending
It adds to retryableRefunds, because success resets the counter
It adds to stuckRefunds alone, as its attempts are above twelve
It adds to pendingRefunds and stuckRefunds, like a pending row

items.explanation: All three refund predicates include x.State == "pending", so a succeeded row is historical success, not recovery work, whatever its attempt count.
